title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio — Scripture senses (nation / office)
pass_a_gloss: 2. Now let us come to the explanation of those three vocabularies which will repeatedly recur in our whole future disputation. The first is Election: Which vocabulary is used diversely in the sacred Scriptures. For sometimes it designates the separation of some nation, unto the common participation of the word and of other means by which human beings are ordinarily led through unto salvation. So God is said to have elected the nation of the Jews, other nations having been passed by. Jehovah your God elected you, that you might be a peculiar people before all peoples, etc. Deuteronomy 7:6. Sometimes this voice denotes the separation of some certain person unto some charge or office either in the commonwealth or in the church. So God is said to have elected Saul into king of the Jews: See whom Jehovah has elected, 1 Samuel 10:24. And Christ thus elected the twelve into Apostles: Did I not elect you twelve, John 6:70. Concerning these elections it is not now inquired: although also in these and the rest of this sort it is permitted to observe that election always signifies the separation of someone or of some from the number of many unto a special end intended by the agent.
pass_b_english: 2. Let us now explain the three words that will keep returning through the whole dispute ahead. First is Election. Scripture uses that word in more than one way. Sometimes it means setting a people apart to share the word and the ordinary means by which people are led to salvation. So God is said to have chosen the Jewish nation and passed by the other nations. "The Lord your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, out of all the peoples," and so on ([[Deuteronomy 7:6 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 7:6]]). Sometimes the same word means setting a particular person apart for an office in the state or in the church. So God is said to have chosen Saul as king of the Jews: "See whom the Lord has chosen" ([[1 Samuel 10:24 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10:24]]); and Christ chose the Twelve as apostles: "Did I not choose you, the twelve?" ([[John 6:70 >> Bible:John 6:70]]). Those elections are not our question now. Still, in them and in every case of the same kind, election always means taking someone — or some — out of a larger number for a special end the agent intends.
source_text: 2. Jam veniamus ad explicationem illorum trium vocabulorum, quae subinde recurrent in tota nostra futura disputatione. Primum est Electio: Quod vocabulum in sacris Scripturis diversimode usurpatur. Nam aliquando designat separationem alicujus gentis, ad participationem communem verbi & aliorum mediorum, quibus homines ordinare perducuntur ad salutem. Sic Deus elegisse dicitur nationem Judaeorum, aliis gentibus praeteritis. Te elegit Jehovah Deus tuus, ut sis populus peculiaris prae omnibus populis, &c. Deut. vii.6. Aliquando vox haec denotat separationem certae alicujus personae ad munus aliquod sive officium vel in Republica vel in ecclesia. Sic Deus dicitur Saulum elegisse in regem Judaeorum: Videte quem elegerit Jehovah, 1 Sam. x.24. & Christus duodecim sic elegit in Apostolos: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi, Johan. vi.70. De hisce electionibus non jam quaeritur: quamvis & in his ac caeteris ejusmodi, observare liceat electionem semper significare alicujus aut aliquorum e numero plurium separationem ad specialem finem ab agente intentum.
